content.title: About
content.content: Seaweed (laminaria) are edible marine algae cultivated in seawater. In this form it is cooked without added fat, retaining a mild flavor and a slightly crunchy texture. It is used in Asian cuisine, salads, soups, and as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seaweed is a rich source of iodine, essential for thyroid function.
In Japan it is called “nori” and is commonly used to wrap sushi.
Laminaria can grow up to 30 meters in its natural habitat.
Commercial cultivation began in China more than 2,000 years ago.
Dried seaweed can be stored for up to a year without losing nutrients.

items.title: High in iodine
items.content: Iodine supports hormonal balance and metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients such as fucoidan help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A serving provides fewer than 30 kcal, making it ideal for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B9 (folate) and small amounts of B12 aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Calcium, iron, magnesium and potassium contribute to bone health and nerve function.

items.title: Excess iodine
items.content: Too much intake may cause hyperthyroidism in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed seaweed can contain elevated sodium levels.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may be allergic to marine algae.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Seaweed can accumulate heavy metals; choose products from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked seaweed can be added to salads, soups, rice or noodle dishes, and used as a garnish. Before serving, rinse it briefly with cold water to remove excess salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 5 days. Dried seaweed should be stored in a cool, dry, dark place.
